reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents with a painful red eye, photophobia, watering, discharge, and reduced vision, usually developing over hours to days
Examination shows a focal white or grey corneal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect that stains with fluorescein; a hypopyon may be present in severe cases
Contact lens wear (especially overnight or poor hygiene) is the leading risk factor, alongside corneal trauma, ocular surface disease, and previous surgery
Pseudomonas is an important and rapidly destructive pathogen in contact lens wearers; Staphylococci and Streptococci are also common
Corneal scraping for Gram stain and culture should ideally be taken before starting intensive treatment in significant ulcers
Management is with intensive topical broad-spectrum antibiotics, initially given very frequently, and stopping contact lens use
Central ulcers, large infiltrates, or delayed treatment risk scarring, perforation, and permanent visual loss
reference.pathophysiology: Bacterial keratitis develops when the corneal epithelial barrier is breached (by trauma, contact lens wear, dry eye, or surgery), allowing bacteria to invade the corneal stroma. Bacterial proliferation and the release of enzymes and toxins, together with the host inflammatory response and recruited neutrophils, cause stromal necrosis and an infiltrate. Collagen-degrading enzymes can rapidly thin the cornea, leading to ulceration, descemetocele formation, and perforation. Healing occurs with scarring that reduces corneal clarity, particularly when the visual axis is involved.
additionalDifferentials: Anterior uveitis or acute angle-closure glaucoma (for the red painful eye)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining to define the infiltrate and epithelial defect
Corneal scraping for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivities
Contact lens and lens case cultures where relevant
Measurement of infiltrate size and assessment of corneal thinning
Confocal microscopy or specialised staining if Acanthamoeba or fungal infection is suspected
redFlags: Sight-threatening — central or large ulcers can scar the visual axis or perforate the cornea
Rapid progression, especially in a contact lens wearer, suggesting Pseudomonas
Hypopyon, corneal thinning, or descemetocele indicating impending perforation
Worsening despite treatment raising suspicion of fungal or Acanthamoeba infection
reference.prognosis: Prompt intensive antibiotic treatment usually controls infection, but a central scar, large ulcer, or delayed care can leave permanent visual impairment; perforation may require corneal grafting.
pitfalls: Prescribing topical steroids or a patch that can worsen infection, particularly with undiagnosed herpetic or fungal disease
Failing to scrape a significant ulcer for culture before starting treatment
Underestimating the aggressiveness of contact-lens-associated Pseudomonas keratitis
Missing Acanthamoeba in a contact lens wearer with pain out of proportion to signs
management: Take a corneal scrape for Gram stain and culture, then start intensive topical broad-spectrum antibiotics such as fluoroquinolone monotherapy or fortified aminoglycoside plus cephalosporin
Administer drops very frequently including overnight in significant ulcers, tapering according to clinical response and culture sensitivities
Stop contact lens wear immediately and send the lens and case for culture
Provide analgesia and a cycloplegic drop for pain and ciliary spasm, and withhold topical corticosteroids until infection is controlled
Monitor infiltrate size, epithelial healing and corneal thinning closely, watching for descemetocele formation and perforation
Escalate to tissue adhesive, corneal glue or emergency keratoplasty for impending or actual perforation
Refer for specialist microscopy and tailored therapy when Acanthamoeba or fungal keratitis is suspected, particularly in unresponsive contact-lens-related disease
